questions.topic: Inequalities and Their Basic Properties
questions.question: If \( a > b \), which of the following must be true?
questions.explanation: Multiplying both sides of \( a > b \) by \(-1\) reverses the inequality: \( -a < -b \). This is the fundamental sign-flip rule for inequalities.
questions.hint: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction.
distractor_logic: This assumes reciprocals can be taken freely, but reciprocals reverse inequalities only under matching-sign conditions, so this comparison isn't guaranteed from \(a>b\) alone.
This assumes squaring preserves the inequality, which fails when \(a\) and \(b\) can be negative — e.g. \(a=1, b=-5\) satisfies \(a>b\) but \(a^2=1 < 25=b^2\).
This keeps the original direction of the inequality instead of reversing it, which is what happens when you forget that multiplying both sides by \(-1\) flips the sign.

questions.topic: Inequalities and Their Basic Properties
questions.question: For real numbers \(a, b, c\), which statement is always true?
options: If \( a > b \), then \( a + c > b + c \) for every real \(c\)
If \( a > b \), then \( \frac{a}{c} > \frac{b}{c} \) for every real \(c\)
If \( a > b \), then \( ac > bc \) for every real \(c\)
If \( a > b \), then \( a - c > c - b \) for every real \(c\)
questions.explanation: Adding the same real number \(c\) to both sides of an inequality never changes its direction, since translation preserves order on the real number line.
questions.hint: Addition/subtraction of the same quantity on both sides always preserves direction — multiplication/division does not, unless you know the sign.
distractor_logic: This fails when \(c\) is negative (it reverses the inequality) and is undefined when \(c=0\), so it cannot hold for every real \(c\).
This is false whenever \(c\) is negative or zero — for example \(a=3, b=1, c=-1\) gives \(ac=-3\) and \(bc=-1\), so \(ac < bc\), not \(ac>bc\).
This mismatches the terms; adding \(-c\) to \(a>b\) only gives \(a-c>b-c\), not this rearranged form.

questions.topic: Inequalities and Their Basic Properties
questions.question: Which operation is guaranteed to preserve the direction of an inequality \( a > b \)?
options: Taking the reciprocal of both sides
Multiplying both sides by any nonzero real number
Adding the same real number to both sides
questions.explanation: Addition/subtraction by any real constant shifts both sides equally and never changes which one is larger, so the inequality direction is always preserved.
questions.hint: Think about which operations can change the relative order of two numbers on the number line.
distractor_logic: Taking reciprocals reverses the inequality only when both sides share the same sign, and is undefined when either side is zero, so it isn't universally safe.
Squaring can reverse the inequality when the numbers involved are negative, e.g. \(-1 > -3\) but \((-1)^2=1 < 9=(-3)^2\).
Multiplying by a negative nonzero number (e.g. \(-2\)) reverses the direction, so 'any nonzero real number' is not safe.

questions.topic: Inequalities and Their Basic Properties
questions.question: If \( a \geq b \) and \( c > 0 \), what can you conclude about \( ac \) and \( bc \)?
options: No relation can be determined without knowing the exact values of \(a\) and \(b\)
questions.explanation: Multiplying a non-strict inequality \( a \geq b \) by a positive number \(c\) preserves both the direction and the possibility of equality: \( ac \geq bc \).
questions.hint: A positive multiplier never changes an inequality's direction, and it preserves \(\geq\) as \(\geq\), not as strict \(>\).
distractor_logic: This drops the possibility of equality; since the original relation is \(\geq\) (not strict), equality can persist (e.g. \(a=b\)), so strict \(ac>bc\) isn't guaranteed.
This reverses the inequality, which only happens when multiplying by a negative number — but here \(c>0\).
The sign of \(c\) alone is enough to determine the direction of the resulting inequality — the exact values of \(a,b\) aren't needed.

questions.question: If \( a < b \) and \( c < 0 \), which is correct?
questions.explanation: Multiplying both sides of \( a < b \) by a negative number \(c\) reverses the inequality, giving \( ac > bc \).
questions.hint: Negative multipliers flip the inequality sign; the rule is different from adding/subtracting a negative number.

Subtracting the same \(c\) from both sides of \(a<b\) preserves \(a-c<b-c\); this confuses the rule for subtraction with the rule for multiplication.
Equality would only hold if \(c=0\), but here \(c<0\), so \(ac\) and \(bc\) remain unequal (in fact strictly reversed).

questions.explanation: A strict inequality uses only \(<\) or \(>\), excluding the equality case; \( 3x-1>5 \) is strict because it uses \(>\).
questions.hint: Strict inequalities use only \(<\) or \(>\); \(\leq\) and \(\geq\) are non-strict because they allow equality.

The \(\geq\) symbol includes the possibility of equality, which makes it non-strict (slack), not strict.

questions.question: By the trichotomy property, for any two real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), exactly one of which statements holds?
options: Only \( a \neq b \) can be concluded
\( a \leq b \) and \( a \geq b \) simultaneously
\( a < b \) and \( a = b \) simultaneously
questions.explanation: The trichotomy property states that for any real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), exactly one of \( a<b \), \( a=b \), \( a>b \) is true.
questions.hint: Trichotomy is about comparability of real numbers — think of the three mutually exclusive ways two numbers can relate.
distractor_logic: Trichotomy gives more than mere inequality — it guarantees exactly one of \(<, =, >\) applies, not just that the numbers might differ.
This isn't how trichotomy is stated — trichotomy names three mutually exclusive relations (\(<,=,>\)), not two combined non-strict ones.
Trichotomy states exactly one relation holds at a time, so \(a<b\) and \(a=b\) cannot both be true simultaneously.

questions.question: Given \( x > y \) and both \(x, y\) are negative, which is true about \( x^2 \) and \( y^2 \)?
options: Cannot be determined without specific values
questions.explanation: If both \(x\) and \(y\) are negative with \(x>y\) (so \(x\) is closer to zero), then \(|x|<|y|\), and squaring gives \(x^2<y^2\). For example \(x=-2,y=-5\): \(x^2=4<25=y^2\).
questions.hint: For negative numbers, the one closer to zero is 'larger' but has the smaller square.
distractor_logic: This assumes squaring preserves order as it does for positive numbers, but for negative numbers the order reverses upon squaring.
The sign condition (both negative, with \(x>y\)) fully determines the direction of the squared inequality — specific values aren't needed.
Equal squares would require \(x=-y\) or \(x=y\); this equality is not implied merely by \(x>y\) with both negative, and generally fails.

questions.explanation: Since \( c^2 \geq 0 \) always, and \(a>b\), if \(c^2>0\) then multiplying preserves direction giving \(ac^2>bc^2\), contradicting \(ac^2\leq bc^2\). The only way to avoid this contradiction is \(c^2=0\), i.e. \(c=0\).
questions.hint: Consider what \(c^2\) must be to avoid a contradiction with \(a>b\).
distractor_logic: Since \(c^2\) is always non-negative regardless of the sign of \(c\), a negative \(c\) (with \(c\neq0\)) still gives \(c^2>0\), leading to the same contradiction as \(c>0\).
If \(c>0\) then \(c^2>0\), and multiplying \(a>b\) by a positive \(c^2\) would force \(ac^2>bc^2\), contradicting the given \(ac^2\leq bc^2\).
The contradiction only vanishes in one specific case, so a definite conclusion about \(c\) is actually forced — it isn't left undetermined.

options: Only when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same sign
Yes — this is always true for all real \(a,b\), with no sign restriction needed

questions.hint: Think about whether \(x^3\) is a monotonically increasing function on the entire real line, unlike \(x^2\).

Same-sign restriction isn't required either; for opposite-sign pairs like \(a=2, b=-3\) (\(a>b\)), cubing gives \(8>-27\), so the implication still holds without any sign-matching condition.

topics.name: Inequalities and Their Basic Properties
topics.summary: An inequality compares two expressions using \(<, \leq, >,\) or \(\geq\), unlike an equation which asserts equality. The properties governing how inequalities behave under algebraic operations are the foundation for everything else in this chapter. Adding or subtracting the same real number from both sides of an inequality never changes its direction. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number also preserves the direction, but multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it — this sign-flip rule is the single most important idea in the chapter. Non-strict inequalities (\(\leq,\geq\)) allow equality; strict ones (\(<,>\)) do not. The trichotomy property guarantees that for any two real numbers, exactly one of \(a<b\), \(a=b\), \(a>b\) holds, and the transitive property lets chained comparisons (\(a\geq b\geq c \Rightarrow a\geq c\)) be combined. Squaring or taking reciprocals does NOT always preserve direction — these operations depend on the signs of the numbers involved, which is where most errors occur.
key_formulas: If \(a>b\), then \(a+c>b+c\) for every real \(c\)
If \(a>b\) and \(c>0\), then \(ac>bc\)
If \(a>b\) and \(c<0\), then \(ac<bc\) (direction reverses)
Trichotomy: exactly one of \(a<b,\ a=b,\ a>b\) holds
Transitivity: if \(a\geq b\) and \(b\geq c\), then \(a\geq c\)
topics.worked_example: Given \(a=3,\ b=7\) (so \(a<b\)), find the direction of \(-2a\) versus \(-2b\). Since \(-2<0\), multiplying \(a<b\) by \(-2\) reverses the inequality: \(-2a>-2b\). Check: \(-2(3)=-6\) and \(-2(7)=-14\), and indeed \(-6>-14\).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number
Assuming squaring always preserves order (fails for negative numbers, e.g. \(-1>-3\) but \((-1)^2<(-3)^2\))
Treating \(\leq\) or \(\geq\) as if they exclude the equality case, or treating \(<,>\) as if they include it
Assuming reciprocals preserve order regardless of sign, when in fact this only holds for same-signed numbers

topics.name: Algebraic Solutions of Linear Inequalities in One Variable
topics.summary: Solving a linear inequality in one variable means isolating the variable using the basic properties from the previous topic, just as with equations — except any multiplication or division by a negative number requires flipping the inequality sign. The general method: expand brackets, clear fractions by multiplying through by the LCM of denominators, collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other, then divide by the coefficient of the variable (flipping the sign if that coefficient is negative). Compound inequalities (like \(a<x+b<c\)) are solved by applying the same operation to all three parts simultaneously. Chained inequalities (\(A<B<C\) or \(A<B\leq C\)) are really two separate conditions joined by 'and', so they must be split, solved individually, and then intersected. When a word problem or side-condition adds an extra restriction (such as requiring an integer or natural-number solution), the final answer is the intersection of the algebraic solution set with that restriction.
key_formulas: To clear a fraction, multiply both sides by the LCM of all denominators present
A chain \(A<B\leq C\) splits into \(A<B\) and \(B\leq C\); the solution is where both hold
For \(a\leq x\leq b\), any operation applied to the middle term must be applied identically to both \(a\) and \(b\)
topics.worked_example: Solve \(\frac{2x-1}{3}>3\). Multiply both sides by 3 (positive, no flip): \(2x-1>9\). Add 1: \(2x>10\). Divide by 2: \(x>5\).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to apply an operation to BOTH constants in a compound inequality, or to only one side of the fraction
Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when the final division is by a negative coefficient
Solving only one half of a chained inequality and reporting it as the complete answer
Rounding a fractional bound in the wrong direction when finding the largest/smallest integer solution

topics.name: Graphical Representation of Solutions on the Number Line
topics.summary: Once an inequality is solved algebraically, its solution set can be pictured on a number line. A strict inequality (\(<,>\)) excludes its boundary value and is shown with an OPEN circle; a non-strict inequality (\(\leq,\geq\)) includes its boundary and is shown with a CLOSED (filled) circle. Shading extends in the direction the inequality points: right for 'greater than', left for 'less than'. Compound inequalities produce a bounded segment between two circles (whose types can differ independently), while 'or' conditions (unions) typically produce disjoint pieces — often two outward-pointing rays. Interval notation mirrors this exactly: square brackets \([,]\) mean 'included' (matching a closed circle), and round brackets \((,)\) mean 'excluded' (matching an open circle). Translating fluently between inequality symbol, number-line picture, and interval notation is the core skill of this topic.
key_formulas: \(x<a\): open circle at \(a\), shaded left; \(x\geq a\): closed circle at \(a\), shaded right
\([a,b)\) means \(a\leq x<b\); \((a,b]\) means \(a<x\leq b\)
'And' conditions overlap (intersect) into one connected piece; 'or' conditions combine into a union of pieces
topics.worked_example: Represent \(-2<x\leq5\): open circle at \(-2\) (excluded), closed circle at \(5\) (included), segment shaded between them. Interval notation: \((-2,5]\).
common_mistakes: Using a closed circle for a strict inequality, or an open circle for a non-strict one
Mismatching which bracket (round/square) goes with which endpoint's strictness
Treating an 'or' (union) condition as if it were an 'and' (intersection), producing the wrong shaded region
Forgetting that both endpoints of a compound inequality can have independently different strictness

topics.name: Graphical Solution of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
topics.summary: A linear inequality in two variables, such as \(ax+by\leq c\), is graphed by first drawing its boundary line \(ax+by=c\): solid if the inequality is non-strict (\(\leq,\geq\), since boundary points satisfy it), dashed if strict (\(<,>\), since they don't). Then a convenient test point not on the line — the origin, when possible — is substituted into the inequality; the half-plane containing that point is shaded if the test makes the inequality true, and the opposite half-plane is shaded otherwise. Inequalities in a single variable (like \(x\leq5\) or \(y>2\)) still graph as half-planes in two dimensions: since the other variable is completely unrestricted, the boundary is a vertical or horizontal line extending the one-variable number-line ray into a full half-plane.
key_formulas: Boundary line: solid for \(\leq,\geq\); dashed for \(<,>\)
Test-point method: substitute a point not on the line; shade its side if the inequality holds there
\(x\leq k\): vertical half-plane left of \(x=k\); \(y\geq k\): horizontal half-plane above \(y=k\)
topics.worked_example: Graph \(x+y<5\): boundary line \(x+y=5\), drawn dashed (strict). Testing the origin: \(0+0=0<5\) is true, so the half-plane containing the origin is shaded.
common_mistakes: Drawing a solid line for a strict inequality or a dashed line for a non-strict one
Shading the wrong side because the test-point substitution was computed incorrectly
Confusing a vertical boundary (from an x-only condition) with a horizontal one (from a y-only condition)
Assuming a fixed 'always shade above/below' rule instead of testing a point for each specific inequality

topics.name: Graphical Solution of a System of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
topics.summary: A system of two-variable inequalities requires every inequality to hold at once, so its solution (the 'feasible region') is the intersection — the overlap — of all the individual half-planes, not their union. The feasible region is often a polygon (or an unbounded polygon-like shape), and its corner points (vertices) are found where two of the system's boundary lines cross, provided that crossing point also satisfies every other constraint. Finding these vertices typically means solving pairs of boundary equations simultaneously (by elimination or substitution). A region is unbounded if it stretches infinitely in some direction (impossible to enclose in a finite circle); it is bounded otherwise. A constraint is 'redundant' if removing it doesn't change the feasible region at all — its boundary doesn't actually cut into the region formed by the other constraints.
key_formulas: Feasible region = intersection of all individual half-planes in the system
A corner point is the simultaneous solution of two boundary equations, checked against all other constraints
A point is feasible only if it satisfies EVERY inequality in the system, checked one at a time
topics.worked_example: For the system \(x+y\leq9\), \(x+2y\leq12\), find the corner point where the two lines meet. Subtracting \(x+y=9\) from \(x+2y=12\) gives \(y=3\); substituting back, \(x=6\). Corner point: \((6,3)\).
common_mistakes: Treating a system's solution as the union of the individual regions instead of their intersection
Reporting a boundary-line intersection as a vertex without checking it actually satisfies every other constraint
Testing only some of a system's constraints when checking whether a point is feasible, instead of all of them
Confusing an unbounded feasible region for a bounded one when a constraint only provides a lower (not upper) bound

topics.name: Word Problems and Applications of Linear Inequalities
topics.summary: Word problems test the ability to translate everyday language into a precise inequality and then solve it. Key phrases have exact mathematical meanings: 'at least' means \(\geq\), 'at most' means \(\leq\), 'more than'/'exceeds' means strict \(>\), and 'less than' means strict \(<\); missing this distinction is the most common source of error. Many problems involve a fixed cost plus a variable rate (like a phone bill or delivery charge), a running total that must stay within a range (like a tank's capacity or a budget), or an average that must clear some threshold. After setting up and solving the inequality, real-world constraints often require rounding to a whole number in the correct direction — for a strict '<' upper bound, round DOWN to the nearest integer below the exact boundary; for a strict '>' lower bound, round UP to the nearest integer above it.
key_formulas: 'At least \(k\)' translates to \(x\geq k\); 'at most \(k\)' translates to \(x\leq k\)
'More than \(k\)' translates to \(x>k\) (strict); 'less than \(k\)' translates to \(x<k\) (strict)
Fixed-plus-variable cost: total \(=\) fixed fee \(+\) (rate \(\times\) quantity)
topics.worked_example: A phone plan charges ₹199 plus ₹2/minute; for the bill to stay strictly under ₹399: \(199+2m<399 \Rightarrow 2m<200 \Rightarrow m<100\). Since this is strict, the maximum whole number of minutes is 99, not 100.
common_mistakes: Misreading 'at least' or 'at most' as the strict inequality (or vice versa), reversing whether the boundary value itself is allowed
Rounding a strict-inequality boundary to the wrong whole number (e.g. keeping the exact boundary value when it should be excluded)
Forgetting to subtract a fixed cost, base amount, or already-completed portion before dividing by the variable rate
Setting up the inequality with the wrong direction relative to the real-world requirement (e.g. writing \(\leq\) for a 'must exceed' condition)
